Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Consumer affairs Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures Consumer watchdog Which? set up and accepted payment for fake listing for ‘1 bed apartment in heart of London’ Ben Quinn Wed 2 Sep 2026 03.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 04.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street. A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?. The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically. The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals. View image in fullscreen Police officers patrol outside 10 Downing Street after a cabinet meeting in July. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images The money had still not been refunded more than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity. A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline. Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately. The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said. The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so. The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live. Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.” The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion A Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced. ‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money back Read more “We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.” It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing. An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-l.text: KYIV – At least one person was killed and 34 wounded in Kyiv as the Russian army attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and attack drones overnight, the capital city’s prosecutor’s office reported on Thursday. Overall, 12 Ukrainian regions were under bombardment, authorities said. “Russian ‘humanitarians’ have launched three waves of ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv, using a total of 21. Unfortunately, the city has sustained significant damage and multiple hits, affecting residential buildings, energy infrastructure, a railway station and the metro, shopping centers, and industrial enterprises. Even a monastery is among the damaged sites,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram after the attack. Ukrainian forces reported shooting down 181 out of 210 Russian drones but none of the ballistic missiles. Advertisement Advertisement Zelenskyy said Russia launched its attack “almost immediately” after talks between U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin ended Wednesday. Witkoff left St. Petersburg after praising Vladimir Putin as a “ humanitarian ,” a word U.S. Vice President JD Vance suggested was tied to the release of Stephen Hubbard , a U.S. citizen detained by Russia since 2022. “We’re getting close to ending the war. We may be closer now than ever before,” U.S. President Donald Trump said shortly after the talks. Ukrainian forces said they killed and wounded a record 2,250 Russian soldiers – the largest number of Russian casualties in 24 hours since 2022, Ukrainian Army General Staff said in a press statement sent to POLITICO on Thursday. Also on Thursday, Russia’s defense ministry reported shooting down 808 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions, including Ukrainian occupied territories.

https://www.dw.com/en/krakow-mass-shooti.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PEV8 Prefer DW on Google The attack has been called a terrorist crime by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk Image: Marcin Golba/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement The alleged shooter who went on a shooting rampage in the Polish city of Krakow on Saturday has died two days after being critically wounded by officers, police said on Monday. "We inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died this morning in the hospital," regional police said in a post on X. The man drove past the square in Krakow's Old Town, an area of Poland 's second-largest city visited by many tourists, and carried out the shooting. He continued shooting even after suffering wounds by police officers, according to the authorities. He is also suspected of killing his parents and sister at his family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles), before carrying out the alleged attack in central Krakow. Six people were killed and 15 wounded in the shooting spree by the 24-year-old Polish man who allegedly carried out the attack. The victims were of various nationalities. Three women and one man were Polish, with two other victims being an Austrian woman and a British man. The list of people injured includes people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. The two officers who stopped the assailant also remained in hospital. Poland in mourning The shooting is being investigated as a terrorist offense. While Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the assailant held radical and ultranationalist views, no information has been given as to whether he was a member of any extremist organization. Grief and shock took over Poland after the shooting. The attack's site at the city's central square became a place of commemoration as many people laid candles and flowers. The St. Mary's Trumpet Call, the melody played at Krakow's Main Square every hour, stopped in honor of the victims. This was the first time this happened since World War II . The St. Anne's Church received a wave of mourners who came to attend a service for the victims. Mass shootings are not common in Poland. Some 411,000 hold gun permits across the country, with interest in gun ownership being on the rise.
